turn_text: We'll be right back. Well, I want to get you to elaborate on two things you mentioned, both capital controls and export controls. So in terms of the capital controls, you mentioned this executive order that President Biden put out, kind of putting some restrictions on tech investments. You don't think that has gone far enough. What are you looking to add there through the committee, through the House as a whole?

And let me say it's a positive first step. I just don't think it can be the last step. One, as I mentioned before, I believe in a sector-based approach. I don't think playing whack-a-mole with all these different Chinese companies on all these different lists that different federal government agencies maintain makes sense. We've seen the ability of China to evade the list or even if you have a company on the list like Avic, Avic owns a bunch of subsidiaries that are just as pernicious. And so a list based or company based approach doesn't make sense to me. It has to be sector specific. I would expand the sectors that are in the executive order and not have carve outs for sub sectors. So that's my concern on the sectors. The second thing is just putting treasury in the lead and giving treasury a ton of exemptions and off ramps makes me a little nervous, given treasuries, dovish history on this issue. And I'm not just saying that under the Biden administration, under the Trump administration, that was the case as well. And there was a division in the administration. And Treasury has a habit of slow rolling some more aggressive measures. And I don't think we have the luxury of time, at least that's what the war game illustrated. So eliminating those off-ramps or putting a different agency in the lead makes sense to me. Finally, and what's most difficult is the executive order only deals with active private investment, private equity and venture capital. That's at most 17% of the problem. Most of the money flowing from America to China is via public equity markets or via passive investments, indexes, ETFs, things like that. I think if the principle is that we don't want to fund our own destruction or Chinese technology that could be used in genocide, Then it shouldn't matter whether it's passive or active or public or private. There should be a set of guardrails that apply to all capital outflows. So expanding the different types of capital on which we place restrictions makes sense to me. So those are the three areas where I think the executive order can be improved and strengthened. Regardless, though, I think what's important, and one thing we heard from Wall Street, which gives me hope, is that, of course, Wall Street executives, bankers, major asset managers have a more dovish position on China than I do, on balance. But as long as Congress legislates a solution, and has an appropriate transition period or glide path, I think they could live with it. And what they fear more than anything else is uncertainty and unpredictability. And there's inherent unpredictability in doing this via executive order, because of course, an executive order can disappear with a new administration. And so putting this on a solid legislative foundation, I think is the most essential thing, because it will provide clear red lines for the financial community, and they can adapt to the new regime.
